implementation_notes: Python does not check annotations at runtime, so the placeholder is simply None for any parameter the exercised path never reads, or object() when a distinct sentinel is wanted (it has no attributes and a useful repr); unittest.mock.sentinel.<name> is the named form of the same idea. No class, no toolkit and no configuration is involved - the double only has to satisfy a signature, not an interface - which makes this the pattern's cheapest home. The callee side has a convention instead of a keyword: a leading underscore in the parameter name (_unused) is understood by readers and by mypy as 'deliberately ignored'. Where a suite prefers a real object over None, the stdlib-mock-placeholder variant supplies it; None remains the default because it also fails immediately (AttributeError) the day the path starts reading the parameter.
code_sketch:
session = Session(cfg, clock=None, sink=object())   # neither is read on this path
session.run()

# callee side: the ignored parameter is named with a leading underscore
def on_event(_event, payload): return payload
pitfalls: None passes every annotation but is also the value code uses to mean 'absent': a callee that branches on `is None` or on truthiness takes a different branch than it would with a real collaborator, so the placeholder can exercise a path other than the one intended.

Type checkers (mypy, pyright) reject None for a parameter annotated with a collaborator type, so the dummy needs an Optional annotation, a cast or an explicit sentinel - choose one deliberately instead of sprinkling `# type: ignore`.
A module-level placeholder instance reused across tests is shared state if anything ever mutates it; define placeholders inline at the call site.

variants.name: unittest.mock.Mock used purely as a signature-satisfying placeholder
variants.implementation_notes: Where a constructor is annotated with a concrete collaborator type and the suite prefers an object to exist rather than None, unittest.mock.Mock (stdlib since Python 3.3) supplies a placeholder with no configuration at all: every attribute access and call succeeds, so the parameter is satisfied without implementing the interface. Two guards keep it a dummy rather than a lazy stub - pass spec=Collaborator (or use autospec) so a call to a member that no longer exists fails, and treat any call into the mock as a test bug (mock.assert_not_called() documents the unused assumption). Choose it when the suite already depends on unittest.mock and None would be misleading; prefer None/object() elsewhere, because a spec-less mock is the placeholder form that hides the most.
variants.code_sketch:
from unittest.mock import Mock

sink = Mock(spec=AuditSink)                 # placeholder, no configuration at all
session = Session(cfg, clock=None, sink=sink)
session.run()
sink.log.assert_not_called()                # documents 'this path must not use it'
pitfalls: Without spec, a Mock accepts any attribute: interface drift is invisible and the placeholder silently absorbs calls the test believed never happen.
A Mock stored in a shared fixture keeps recorded calls and child mocks between tests, turning a placeholder into leaked cross-test state.

Mock() is not None: code branching on `is None` gets the absent-value branch, while truthiness checks see a truthy object, so behaviour can differ from the None placeholder in exactly the paths that made you reach for a dummy.
